heading: What is Spring Framework
subheading: A lightweight framework that makes Java enterprise development simpler and loosely coupled
description:
Spring is an open-source dependency injection framework for Java, created by Rod Johnson in 2003. Its primary goal is to make Java EE application development simpler by promoting loose coupling between components.

The core idea behind Spring is Inversion of Control (IoC) — instead of your code creating and managing its own dependencies, the Spring framework takes over that responsibility. You define what objects (beans) your application needs and how they relate to each other, and Spring handles creating them, wiring them together, and managing their lifecycle.

Why Spring?
• Eliminates tightly coupled code — components depend on abstractions, not concrete implementations.
• Reduces boilerplate — Spring handles repetitive infrastructure code (database connections, transaction management, security) so you can focus on business logic.
• Modular architecture — use only the modules you need (Spring MVC for web, Spring Data for databases, Spring Security for auth).
• Testability — loose coupling makes unit testing straightforward with mock objects.
• Massive ecosystem — integrates seamlessly with Hibernate, JPA, Kafka, RabbitMQ, and virtually every Java library.

heading: IoC Container & Dependency Injection
subheading: The heart of Spring — letting the framework create and wire your objects
description:
**IoC Container:**
The IoC (Inversion of Control) Container is the core component of Spring. It is responsible for creating objects (beans), holding them in memory, configuring them, and injecting them wherever they are needed.

To work, the IoC container needs two things:
• Bean definitions — which classes (POJOs) it should manage.
• Configuration — how beans depend on each other.

Implementations of the **IoC Container:**
• **BeanFactory** — the older, lightweight implementation. Creates beans lazily (on demand). Suitable for resource-constrained environments.
• **ApplicationContext** — the modern, feature-rich implementation built on top of BeanFactory. Supports eager initialization, event handling, internationalization, and AOP integration. This is what you use in practice.
  Common types: ClassPathXmlApplicationContext, AnnotationConfigApplicationContext, FileSystemXmlApplicationContext.

**Dependency Injection (DI):**
DI is the design pattern that implements IoC. Instead of a class creating its own dependencies, the framework injects them at runtime. The class simply declares what it needs, and Spring provides it.

Two types of DI:
• **Setter Injection** — dependencies are injected through setter methods after the object is created. Flexible but allows partially constructed objects.
• **Constructor Injection** — dependencies are injected through the constructor when the object is created. Recommended approach because it ensures all required dependencies are provided upfront, making the object immutable and fully initialized.

Configuration can be provided via XML files, Java annotations (@Component, @Autowired), or Java configuration classes (@Configuration, @Bean).

heading: Bean Lifecycle & Scopes
subheading: How Spring creates, initializes, uses, and destroys managed objects
description:
Bean Lifecycle — the stages every Spring-managed object goes through:
1. Load Bean Definition — Spring reads the bean configuration from XML, annotations, or Java config classes.
2. Bean Instantiation — the IoC container creates an instance of the bean using the constructor.
3. Bean Initialization — Spring populates the bean's properties and dependencies as defined in the configuration.
4. Bean Usage — the application retrieves and uses the bean via ApplicationContext.getBean() or dependency injection.
5. Bean Destruction — when the application shuts down, Spring calls the destroy method to release resources.

Bean Scopes — control how many instances of a bean are created:
• **Singleton (default)** — only one instance is created per Spring container and shared across the entire application. Created at startup. Used for stateless components like services, controllers, and repositories.
• **Prototype** — a new instance is created every time the bean is requested. Spring creates it but does not manage its destruction — you must clean it up manually.
• **Request** — one instance per HTTP request. Automatically destroyed when the request completes. Used in web applications.
• **Session** — one instance per HTTP session. Destroyed when the session expires.

**Eager vs Lazy Initialization:**
• **Eager (default)** — beans are created at application startup. Catches configuration errors early but increases startup time.
• **Lazy (@Lazy)** — beans are created only when first requested. Faster startup but errors surface later at runtime.

heading: Spring MVC & Dispatcher Servlet
subheading: Building web applications using the Model-View-Controller pattern with a central request handler
description:
**MVC Design Pattern:**
MVC separates a web application into three layers:
• Model — holds the application data and business logic.
• View — the presentation layer (HTML, JSP, Thymeleaf templates) that renders data for the user.
• Controller — receives user requests, processes them using services, and returns the appropriate response.

Spring Web MVC is the module that implements this pattern. At its core is the Dispatcher Servlet, which acts as the Front Controller — the single entry point for all incoming HTTP requests.

**Request flow through Spring MVC:**
1. Client sends an HTTP request → it hits the Dispatcher Servlet.
2. Dispatcher Servlet consults the Handler Mapping to determine which controller method should handle this request (based on URL patterns and annotations like @RequestMapping).
3. The matched Controller processes the request — executes business logic with the help of Service and Repository layers.
4. The Controller returns a ModelAndView object containing the data (model) and the name of the view to render.
5. Dispatcher Servlet passes the view name to the View Resolver, which locates the actual view template (e.g., /WEB-INF/views/home.jsp).
6. The View is rendered with the model data and sent back to the client as the HTTP response.

Design patterns commonly used in Spring:
• Singleton — one instance per bean (default scope).
• Factory Method — BeanFactory creates beans.
• MVC — separates concerns into model, view, and controller.
• DAO (Data Access Object) — abstracts database access behind a clean interface.

heading: Spring Boot — Overview & Core Principles
subheading: Rapid application development built on top of Spring with sensible defaults
description:
Spring Boot is an open-source framework built on top of the Spring Framework. Its goal is to eliminate the tedious configuration work that traditional Spring applications require, so you can get a production-ready application running in minutes.

**Core Principles:**
• Opinionated Defaults — Spring Boot provides pre-configured settings for Maven/Gradle setup, dependencies, project structure, and common configurations. You get sensible defaults out of the box and only override what you need.
• Convention over Configuration — if you follow established patterns and naming conventions, Spring Boot automatically configures everything for you without explicit setup.
• Auto-Configuration — based on the dependencies on your classpath, Spring Boot automatically configures beans, the Dispatcher Servlet, view resolvers, data sources, and more. No manual XML or Java config needed.
• Embedded Servers — Spring Boot applications come with an embedded web server (Tomcat by default, or Jetty/Undertow). No need to deploy WAR files to an external server — just run the JAR.

What you can build with Spring Boot:
• Web applications and REST APIs.
• Microservices.
• Batch processing jobs.
• Integration with messaging systems (Kafka, RabbitMQ).
• Applications with built-in monitoring and health checks.

heading: Spring Boot Starters
subheading: Pre-packaged dependency bundles that simplify project setup
description:
A Spring Boot Starter is a dependency descriptor — a single dependency you add to your project that automatically pulls in all the libraries, configurations, and version-compatible modules you need for a specific functionality.

**Why starters exist:**
• Simplify configuration — no need to manually find and add dozens of individual JARs.
• Ensure compatibility — all dependencies within a starter are tested to work together.
• Boost productivity — developers focus on business logic instead of dependency management.

Commonly used starters:
• spring-boot-starter — core starter providing auto-configuration, logging, and YAML processing.
• spring-boot-starter-web — everything needed for building web applications: Spring MVC, RESTful services, Jackson (JSON), and an embedded Tomcat server.
• spring-boot-starter-data-jpa — Spring Data JPA, Hibernate, JDBC, and connection pooling for database access.
• spring-boot-starter-test — testing libraries including JUnit 5, Mockito, AssertJ, and Spring Test.
• spring-boot-starter-security — Spring Security for authentication and authorization.
• spring-boot-starter-actuator — production-ready features like health checks, metrics, and application monitoring endpoints.

How it works: when you add spring-boot-starter-web to your pom.xml or build.gradle, Maven/Gradle resolves all transitive dependencies, and Spring Boot's auto-configuration detects them on the classpath and sets everything up automatically.

heading: Spring Boot Startup Flow
subheading: What happens behind the scenes when your Spring Boot application starts
description:
When you run a Spring Boot application, the following sequence occurs:

1. main() method executes — calls SpringApplication.run(), which bootstraps the entire application.
2. Application type detection — Spring Boot determines whether the application is a Servlet-based web app, a Reactive web app, or a non-web application, and loads the appropriate ApplicationContext.
3. Environment preparation — loads configuration properties from application.yml (or .properties), OS environment variables, JVM system properties, and command-line arguments.
4. Banner printing — displays the Spring Boot banner in the console (customizable or can be disabled).
5. @SpringBootApplication processing — this single annotation expands into three:
   • @Configuration — marks the class as a source of bean definitions.
   • @ComponentScan — scans the base package and sub-packages for classes annotated with @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller, etc.
   • @EnableAutoConfiguration — triggers auto-configuration based on classpath dependencies.
6. Bean creation and dependency injection — Spring creates all discovered beans, resolves their dependencies, and injects them.
7. Embedded server startup — the embedded Tomcat (or Jetty/Undertow) server starts and begins listening for HTTP requests.
8. Application ready — the application is fully initialized and ready to serve requests.

heading: Key Spring Boot Annotations
subheading: The annotations that wire your application together
description:
**Core annotations:**
• @SpringBootApplication — the entry point annotation, combining @Configuration + @ComponentScan + @EnableAutoConfiguration. Placed on the main class.
• @Configuration — marks a class as a source of bean definitions. Methods inside annotated with @Bean are called at startup to create and register objects.
• @Bean — placed on a method inside a @Configuration class. Tells Spring to call this method at startup and register the returned object as a bean.
• @ComponentScan — tells Spring which packages to scan for annotated classes. Defaults to the base package of the main class.

**Stereotype annotations** (specializations of @Component):
• @Component — generic annotation marking a class as a Spring-managed bean.
• @Service — marks a class that contains business logic. Functionally identical to @Component but communicates intent.
• @Repository — marks a class as a data access component. Enables automatic exception translation for database errors.
• @Controller — marks a class that handles HTTP requests and can return both data and views.
• @RestController — combines @Controller + @ResponseBody. Returns data (JSON/XML) directly in the response body, skipping view resolution.

**Dependency injection annotations:**
• @Autowired — tells Spring to automatically inject the required dependency. Works by type first, then by name. Constructor injection is recommended.
• @Qualifier — resolves ambiguity when multiple beans of the same type exist. Specifies which bean to inject by name.
• @Primary — marks a bean as the default choice when multiple beans of the same type exist. Eliminates the need for @Qualifier everywhere.

**Web annotations:**
• @RequestMapping — maps HTTP requests to controller methods. Can be used on both class and method level.
• @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping — shorthand annotations for specific HTTP methods.
• @RequestBody — binds the HTTP request body (JSON) to a Java object using HttpMessageConverter.
• @RequestParam — extracts query parameters from the request URL.
• @PathVariable — extracts dynamic values from the URL path.
• @RequestHeader — accesses HTTP request headers.

heading: Spring JDBC & ORM
subheading: Connecting to databases — from raw JDBC to object-relational mapping
description:
**Spring JDBC:**
Spring JDBC is a module that simplifies database access using the standard JDBC API. It handles all the boilerplate — opening connections, preparing statements, processing exceptions, managing transactions, and closing connections — so you only write the SQL and result processing logic.

Key components:
• **DriverManagerDataSource** — an implementation of the DataSource interface (from javax.sql). It loads the database driver, holds connection configuration (URL, username, password), and establishes connections between the application and the database.
• **JdbcTemplate** — the central class for executing SQL operations.
  - update() — for INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE statements.
  - query() — for SELECT statements.

**ORM (Object-Relational Mapping):**
ORM is a technique that maps Java objects directly to database tables. Instead of writing SQL manually, you work with Java objects, and the ORM framework translates your operations into SQL behind the scenes.

Benefits:
• No need to change SQL everywhere when an entity changes — the mapping handles it.
• Automatic migrations and schema generation.
• Built-in session and transaction management.

**Hibernate:**
Hibernate is the most popular ORM framework in Java. It maps Java classes (entities) to database tables and provides:
• Automatic SQL generation — reduces the effort of writing queries.
• Entity management — a Java class annotated with @Entity is mapped to a table.
• SessionFactory — manages database connections and sessions.

**JPA (Java/Jakarta Persistence API):**
JPA is a specification (set of rules and annotations) that standardizes how ORM frameworks like Hibernate interact with databases. Hibernate is the most common JPA implementation.
• JPA defines the standard annotations (@Entity, @Id, @Column, etc.).
• Hibernate provides the actual implementation that executes the mapping.
• Think of it this way: JPA tells you what to do, Hibernate does it.

heading: Spring Data JPA & Repositories
subheading: Eliminating boilerplate data access code with ready-made repository interfaces
description:
Spring Data JPA is an abstraction layer built on top of JPA that dramatically reduces the amount of code needed for database operations. Instead of writing DAO classes with repetitive CRUD logic, you simply define an interface, and Spring generates the implementation at runtime.

Repository types:
• **CrudRepository** — provides basic CRUD operations: save(), findById(), findAll(), deleteById(). No pagination or sorting support.
• **JpaRepository** — extends CrudRepository with additional features: batch operations (saveAll(), deleteAllInBatch()), pagination and sorting, flush operations, and derived query methods.

**Derived Query Methods:**
Spring Data JPA can generate queries automatically from method names. You just declare a method in your repository interface, and Spring parses the name into a query.
• findByEmail(String email) → SELECT * FROM user WHERE email = ?
• findByUsernameAndStatus(String username, String status) → SELECT * FROM user WHERE username = ? AND status = ?

**Query languages:**
• JPQL (Jakarta Persistence Query Language) — a database-independent, object-oriented query language. Queries are written against Java entities (not database tables), making them portable across different databases. Hibernate translates JPQL into native SQL at runtime.
• Native Queries — pure SQL written directly against database tables. Database-specific and not portable, but useful for complex queries that JPQL cannot express efficiently.

Example:
@Query("SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.status = :status") — JPQL query.
@Query(value = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE status = :status", nativeQuery = true) — Native SQL query.

heading: Entity Mapping & Relationships
subheading: Mapping Java classes to database tables and defining how they relate
description:
**Entity vs Table:**
• A table is a database concept — rows and columns stored on disk.
• An entity is a JPA concept — a Java class that represents a table in code.

Key annotations:
• @Entity — marks a Java class as a JPA entity. Required by Hibernate for mapping the class to a database table.
• @Id — marks a field as the primary key. Every entity must have exactly one @Id field.
• @GeneratedValue — tells JPA to auto-generate primary key values. Strategies:
  - IDENTITY — uses the database's auto-increment feature.
  - SEQUENCE — uses a database sequence object.
  - AUTO — lets JPA choose the best strategy for the underlying database.

Relationship annotations:
• @OneToMany — one entity is associated with many instances of another entity (e.g., one department has many employees).
• @ManyToOne — the inverse of @OneToMany (e.g., many employees belong to one department).
• @OneToOne — one entity is associated with exactly one instance of another.
• @ManyToMany — many instances of one entity relate to many instances of another.

**Fetch Types:**
• Lazy Fetching (default for collections) — related data is loaded only when it is actually accessed. Uses proxy objects. More efficient for large datasets.
• Eager Fetching (default for single associations) — related data is loaded immediately along with the parent entity. Simpler but can cause performance issues if relationships are deep.

**N+1 Problem:**
A common performance issue with Hibernate. When fetching a parent entity with a @OneToMany relationship using lazy loading, Hibernate executes 1 query to fetch the parent and then N additional queries to fetch each child — resulting in N+1 total queries. Solutions include using JOIN FETCH in JPQL, @EntityGraph, or batch fetching.

heading: Bean Validation
subheading: Declaratively validating request data using annotations
description:
Bean Validation provides a clean, declarative way to validate incoming request data without writing manual validation logic. You annotate fields in your request DTO with constraint annotations, and the framework validates them automatically.

Common validation annotations:
• @NotNull — the field must not be null.
• @NotBlank — the string must not be null, empty, or whitespace-only.
• @Size(min, max) — the string/collection length must be within the specified range.
• @Min(value) / @Max(value) — the numeric value must be at least / at most the specified value.
• @Pattern(regexp) — the string must match the given regular expression.
• @Email — the string must be a valid email format.

How to use:
1. Annotate the fields in your request DTO class with the appropriate constraint annotations.
2. Add @Valid on the request body parameter in your controller method — this triggers validation.
3. If validation fails, Spring automatically returns a 400 Bad Request with error details.

@Valid vs @Validated:
• @Valid — standard Java Bean Validation annotation. Triggers validation on the annotated object.
• @Validated — Spring-specific annotation that supports group validation, allowing you to apply different validation rules in different contexts (e.g., different rules for create vs update).

Under the hood, Spring uses Hibernate Validator as the default implementation of the Bean Validation specification.

heading: Spring Batch
subheading: Processing large volumes of data efficiently with chunk-based jobs
description:
Spring Batch is a Spring module designed for processing massive amounts of data reliably and at high speed. It is used for ETL jobs, report generation, data migration, and any scenario where you need to process millions of records.

Key features:
• Chunk Processing — breaks large datasets into smaller chunks and processes them incrementally. If a failure occurs, only the affected chunk needs to be reprocessed, not the entire dataset.
• Scheduled Execution — jobs can be triggered on a schedule (e.g., nightly data processing, weekly reports).
• Error Handling & Retry — if a step fails, it can be retried a configurable number of times or skipped entirely.
• Restartability — if a job fails midway, it can be restarted from where it left off rather than from the beginning.
• Job Monitoring — Spring Batch maintains a built-in Job Repository that tracks the status, start time, end time, and outcome of every job execution.

Spring Batch Architecture:
• Job Launcher — an interface that triggers job execution. You call it programmatically or via a scheduler.
• Job — represents the entire batch process. A job consists of one or more sequential steps. Each job has a JobInstance (logical run identity) and JobExecution (physical run record).
• Step — an independent, sequential phase within a job. Each step has three components:
  - ItemReader — reads data from a source (database, file, API).
  - ItemProcessor — transforms, filters, or applies business logic to each item.
  - ItemWriter — writes the processed data to a destination (database, file, message queue).
• Job Repository — the audit log that Spring Batch maintains automatically. It stores metadata about every job and step execution, enabling monitoring, restart capability, and history tracking.
